summary: Two towers side by side at the mouth of Chesapeake Bay: the 1792 sandstone original, first lighthouse built by the federal government, and the 1881 black-and-white cast-iron light still in service.

access.note: Both towers are inside Joint Expeditionary Base Fort Story. The old tower is open Tuesday to Sunday on guided, timed tickets with a base security form; the new tower is closed to the public.

corrections.current: tower, cast_iron, built 1792, 15.5 m; tower, brick, built 1950, 25.0 m
corrections.proposed: Old tower: octagonal sandstone, built 1792, 72 ft (22 m) of stonework. New tower: cast iron, built 1881, 157-165 ft (48-50 m). No source read mentions a brick tower of 1950.
corrections.why: The record's first structure pairs the 1792 date with cast iron; the 1792 tower is sandstone and the cast-iron tower is of 1881.
1791 is the year the contract was signed and work began; the light was first shown in 1792 (October, per the nomination).

corrections.proposed: New tower first lit 15 December 1881; the old tower's light was discontinued the same night and the tower kept as a daymark
corrections.why: The record attaches both 1881 events to one station; they belong to the two towers.

resolved_conflicts.explanation: The record says sources differ on whether the light is still lit. The old tower's light ended in 1881; the cast-iron tower is described in August 2026 as still in service.

The record's two towers are different structures. For the cast-iron tower the Light-House Board's description gives 157 feet and Putnam 1917 gives 165 feet; LighthouseFriends gives 157 feet as the focal plane in 1881, so the figures may measure different things.

The archive roster begins with William Lewis (1792), LighthouseFriends says Washington appointed Lewis who died a month later, and the 1939 Bulletin says the first keeper appears to have been Laban Goffigan, known to be serving in 1794.

notes_for_editor: Rich station but the Light-House Board reports for 1872-1890 and the Board's account of the 1881 construction are not in the local corpus, so the construction story rests on LighthouseFriends (which cites those reports) and the 1939 and 1930 Bulletins; a reviewer with the 1880 and 1881 Board reports should check the pier collapse and tower dates. The roster is the USLHS list from NARA registers; it is not confirmed in a primary record. Disagreements: (a) automation 1983 (USLHS) / 1984 (LighthouseFriends) / last keeper retired 1999 (Preservation Virginia marker); (b) Ephraim H. Riggs principal keeper from 1907 (USLHS) or 1908 (LighthouseFriends); (c) first keeper (see resolved_conflicts); (d) the old tower is 'third oldest' (NRHP nomination) or 'fourth oldest' (LighthouseFriends) standing lighthouse; (e) the marker says the 1881 tower was shipped by barge from Philadelphia, LighthouseFriends says materials came by pier and tramway via Lynnhaven Inlet. Efficiency pennant: the Cape Henry / E. H. Riggs match in the 1914 Bulletin list was made by column position (fifth district, fifth keeper name) and is confirmed by the 1912-17 index entry; the checker should read the page image. Newspaper spellings of the keeper vary (Odell, O'Dell, with initials W. L., W. T., M. L. in OCR); the roster gives Milton L. Odell. The complainant Philip Morrissett of Norfolk (also William Morrisett, who swore out the 1888 perjury warrant) resembles the roster's Philip Morrisett, first assistant in 1886, but no source connects them, so the story does not. The Jefferson endorsement of 31 December 1806 does not name the keeper; the roster shows Henry James until 1807 but no source ties him to it. Albion item (Nebraska Advertiser, 30 May 1861) is a second-hand wartime report; it says 'lighthouse' removed, not what was removed.
